question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (4y-100)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Now, we let $u=4y-100.$ Then differentiating with respect to $y$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}y=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $y$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4y-100)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {u}^{-1/2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{(1/2)}{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{4}\cdot {u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4y-100)^{1/2}+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4y-100}}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\frac{\sqrt{4y-100}}{2}+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\sqrt{4y-100}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[(4y-100)^{1/2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(4y-100)^{-1/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(4y-100)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4y-100)^{-1/2}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4y-100}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (5x-1)^{1/2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we let $u=5x-1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5x-1)^{1/2}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{1/2}\cdot (\frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(5x-1)^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(5x-1)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(5x-1)^{3}}+C] & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\sqrt{(5x-1)^{3}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(5x-1)^{3/2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{3}{2}(5x-1)^{1/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x-1)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(5x-1)^{1/2}\cdot 5 \\  & =(5x-1)^{1/2} \\  & =\sqrt{5x-1}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x-63)^{7/4}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{7/4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{11/4}}{11/4}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{11}(x-63)^{11/4}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{11}\sqrt[4]{(x-63)^{11}}+C\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int {(s+1)}^{-3/5}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, we let  $u=s+1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $s$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}s}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}s=\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $s$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(s+1)}^{-3/5}\,\text{d}s & =\int {u}^{-3/5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2/5}{u}^{2/5}+C \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{u}^{2/5}+C \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{(s+1)}^{2/5}+C \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\sqrt[5]{{(s+1)}^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}[\frac{5}{2}\sqrt[5]{{(s+1)}^{2}}+C] & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}[\sqrt[5]{{(s+1)}^{2}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(C) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}[{(s+1)}^{2/5}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(C) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{(s+1)}^{-3/5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(s+1)+0 \\  & ={(s+1)}^{-3/5}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{{(s+1)}^{3}}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
